title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
raw_text: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed. title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
raw_text: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs. The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. “Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed. The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field. “Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. title: Steering AI Beyond Automation
raw_text: By Gabriel Unger and Arvind Narayanan. Unger is an economist at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. One of the most fundamental questions for the field of AI today is: to what extent is the project of AI purely about automating human labor? The dominant Silicon Valley program for AI right now, with both industry and academic faces, answers: “almost entirely.” 1 There is an implicit technological determinism: that AI has a deep internal logic that favors automation. To keep pushing in this direction is to move towards economic growth, prosperity, and profit. The vision of AGI is the successful completion of this project: to create AI systems capable enough to autonomously do everything a human can do. There is an alternative view : that AI is a technology (or class of technologies) that, like any technology, can develop in different directions. Total automation is one direction. But there are others, including directions that focus more on human augmentation, and increasing the collaborative and collective power of teams of humans and AI models working together. This view — our view — is not that automation is never good. Clearly sometimes it is, and clearly sometimes some subset of people try to oppose it out of the narrowest short-term self interest, at the expense of broader social and economic progress. title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
raw_text: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

title: Report: Between Google Scholar and ChatGPT: How Economics and Business Students Conduct Research in 2026
raw_text: From ZBW (Leibniz Information Centre for Economics) MediaTalk: Students in economics and business studies today draw on a wide range of information environments when searching for academic literature. Google Scholar, library catalogues and generative AI are part of their everyday research routines. But what role do traditional subject-specific databases still play? And how well do students manage to find information, assess its quality and use it correctly in an academic context? These questions are at the heart of our new study (in German) „Zwischen Google Scholar und ChatGPT – Wie Wirtschaftsstudierende heute recherchieren“ (“Between Google Scholar and ChatGPT – How economics and business students conduct research today”). Between March and May 2026, we conducted an online survey of 908 economics and business students at German universities. Research habits are shifting The results show, first of all, that independent literature searching is routine for the vast majority of the surveyed students: 88.3 per cent have searched for literature or specialist information on their own, either frequently or occasionally. General search engines remain the most widely used tools, with 91.3 per cent of those with research experience using Google, Google Scholar or similar services sometimes or often. title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
raw_text: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The US military’s race to make fake blood In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply. Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield. The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives. title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
raw_text: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2. In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off. As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed. Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer. Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
raw_text: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. raw_text: Direct to Full Text Report: The State of U.S. Academic Libraries: Findings From the ACRL 2025 Annual Survey 25 pages; PDF. From an ACRL Post: This report focuses on U.S. academic libraries in fiscal year 2025 (the 2024–25 academic year). With the sunset of the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) Academic Libraries component after FY 2024, ACRL’s annual survey is the only source of comprehensive, national data. The results are weighted and therefore representative of all U.S. academic libraries. Key findings include: Library Staff: The median total full-time equivalent (FTE) staff is 7.6, a slight decrease relative to 2024 even as the ratio of FTE students to staff has risen. Expenditures : Median total annual library expenditures are $470 thousand, excluding fringe benefits. Libraries spend $523 per student FTE, the same as in 2024, suggesting that when adjusted for inflation, libraries have less spending power in real terms. Collections and circulation: Academic libraries continue to focus on electronic resources, with 79.7% of total collection holdings and 98.2% of total circulation in digital format. Visits: The number of people entering academic libraries annually increased by about ten percent in 2025 relative to 2024, reaching a median of 53,250. Information Services: Library staff share expertise through interactions with users one-on-one and in groups. title: In Memoriam: Jan-Ewout van der Putten
raw_text: Op 30 september 2026 overleed Jan-Ewout van der Putten, 78 jaar oud. Als secretaris-directeur van eerst de Vereniging NBLC en later de Vereniging van Openbare Bibliotheken was hij bijna elf jaar nauw betrokken bij de ontwikkeling van het Nederlandse openbare bibliotheekwerk. Samenwerking en inhoudelijke vernieuwing stonden daarbij voor hem voorop. In onderstaande tekst leest u twee in memoriam-artikelen. Tekst 1: Eimer Wieldraaijer Toen Van der Putten in februari 1999 aantrad bij de Vereniging NBLC, bracht hij een ruime bestuurlijke ervaring mee. Hij was tien jaar plaatsvervangend griffier van de Eerste Kamer geweest en vervolgens zes jaar wethouder voor D66 in Den Haag. Hij kende de politieke besluitvorming van binnenuit: een waardevolle achtergrond voor een sector waarin gemeenten, provincies en rijksoverheid ieder hun eigen verantwoordelijkheden en belangen hadden. Zijn directeurschap viel samen met een ingrijpende periode van bibliotheekvernieuwing. De vorming van basisbibliotheken, veranderende bestuurlijke verhoudingen en de ontwikkeling van digitale dienstverlening vroegen om richting en afstemming. Van der Putten behoorde tot de landelijke hoofdrolspelers in dat proces. Ook droeg hij bij aan een nieuwe structuur voor het blindenbibliotheekwerk en de verbinding daarvan met het reguliere openbare bibliotheekwerk. title: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
raw_text: If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten. — Geoffrey Huntley , nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left. title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
raw_text: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. title: Metropolitan Libraries Spotlight: How Nanhai Library Is Reconnecting Children with the Classics
raw_text: When a thousand-year-old novel has to compete with a 15-second video In Foshan, in the heart of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Nanhai Library serves a district of more than 3.7 million people, where local families, migrant workers, students, and seniors intertwine in a fast-moving, diverse community. It is also a community facing a very contemporary problem: as short-form video quietly absorbs every spare moment of screen time, deep reading is being pushed to the margins, even when the content at stake is centuries old. Rather than treat this as a lost cause, the library decided to meet children where their attention already lives. In April 2026, it launched Classics 101: Mental Models for Kids, a program built specifically for 10- to 12-year-olds — the exact age when children move from picture-to-text bridge books into more demanding reading. Making the classics legible again The challenge was concrete and specific. More than 60% of students in the first sessions admitted their biggest frustration was simple: they could not remember who everyone was or how all the characters connected. The semi-archaic language, sprawling character webs, and unhurried pacing of China’s Four Great Classical Novels were never designed to compete with instant gratification. So Nanhai Library stopped asking children to memorize plots and started extracting something more useful: practical mental models drawn directly from the characters’ journeys. title: Forse Vlaamse besparingen treffen erfgoedbibliotheken, archieven en kwetsbare lezers hard
raw_text: De drastische besparingsplannen van de nieuwe Vlaamse regering slaan diepe wonden in de archief- en bibliotheeksector. Naast het nieuws dat landelijke erfgoedbibliotheken hun volledige structurele subsidies verliezen en archieven de helft moeten inleveren, luiden nu ook de informatieopleidingen en de sector voor passend lezen de noodklok. In twee brandbrieven waarschuwen de Arteveldehogeschool en Luisterpuntbibliotheek voor onomkeerbare schade aan het Vlaamse geheugen en de toegankelijkheid van informatie. Ook de VVBAD (Vlaamse Vereniging voor Bibliotheek, Archief & Documentatie ), Openbare Bibliotheek Brugge , Universiteitsbibliotheek Gent en Erfgoedbibliotheek Hendrik Conscience roepen op tot actie. Binnen het nieuwe begrotingsakkoord van minister van Cultuur Caroline Gennez moet de cultuur- en erfgoedsector vanaf 1 januari 2027 structureel 47 miljoen euro besparen. Voor de grote landelijke erfgoedbibliotheken – de Hendrik Conscience-erfgoedbibliotheek in Antwerpen, de Openbare Bibliotheek Brugge en de Gentse Boekentoren – betekent dit dat zij 100 procent van hun jaarlijkse Vlaamse subsidies kwijtspelen, een verlies van zo’n 1 miljoen euro. Erkende stadsarchieven en instellingen zoals het AMVB in Brussel zien hun middelen gehalveerd. title: Eerste Haagse school start met de Bibliotheek op school Plus
raw_text: De Annie M.G. Schmidtschool is de eerste school in Den Haag die start met de Bibliotheek op school Plus (dBos+). In deze intensieve samenwerking werken de school, Bibliotheek Den Haag en ABC Onderwijsadviseurs de komende twee jaar aan het versterken van leesplezier, leesbegrip en leesonderwijs. De officiële aftrap vond plaats tijdens de opening van de Kinderb Kinderen die met plezier lezen, ontwikkelen niet alleen hun taalvaardigheid, maar vergroten ook hun kansen om mee te doen in de samenleving en nieuwe perspectieven te ontdekken. dBos+ is een verdiepende aanpak binnen het landelijke programma de Bibliotheek op school dat inmiddels op ruim 70 Haagse scholen van start is gegaan. Naast een actuele en aantrekkelijke schoolbibliotheek krijgen scholen extra ondersteuning van Bibliotheek Den Haag bij het versterken van hun leesbeleid, het vergroten van de leesmotivatie van leerlingen en het verder ontwikkelen van de leesvaardigheid. Lezen opent nieuwe werelden Tijdens de feestelijke opening stonden boeken en verhalen centraal. Leerlingen voerden het Kinderboekenweeklied uit en gaven met vertegenwoordigers van de school, Bibliotheek Den Haag en ABC Onderwijsadviseurs het officiële startsein voor de Kinderboekenweek en dBos+. title: includi herontwerpt centrale bibliotheek van Grand Rapids Public Library (GRPL) in Michigan
raw_text: (Meer foto’s onder aan het artikel) Samen met inwoners en medewerkers werkt includi aan de vernieuwing van de centrale bibliotheek van Grand Rapids Public Library in Michigan (VS). Zo ontstaat een uitnodigende bibliotheek die meegroeit met de stad. Het project richt zich op het vernieuwen van de historische entreehal, de jeugdafdelingen en de gemeenschappelijke ruimtes op de benedenverdieping. Deze ruimtes worden getransformeerd tot een hoogwaardige third place: een plek waar mensen graag samenkomen. Hiermee versterkt GRPL haar rol als ontmoetingsplek die inwoners verbindt, waar zij zich thuis voelen en trots op kunnen zijn. Het resultaat wordt een vernieuwde bibliotheek waar iedereen zich welkom voelt. Een plek om boeken te lenen, te studeren, activiteiten bij te wonen of rustig de krant te lezen, alleen of samen met anderen. Een bibliotheek waar mensen willen blijven “We zien bibliotheken als echte third places (derde plekken): laagdrempelige publieke plekken naast huis en werk waar mensen elkaar ontmoeten. Hun deuren staan wijd open en nodigen mensen uit om binnen te komen. Ze bieden het comfort en de sfeer waardoor mensen willen blijven. En ze geven mensen de kans om te groeien. Hoe een bibliotheek eruitziet doet ertoe, maar wat mensen er kunnen doen en beleven is nog belangrijker. We vinden het een eer om Grand Rapids Public Library te helpen haar ambitie als ontmoetingsplek voor de stad waar te maken en kijken uit naar de samenwerking,” vertelt Aat Vos, creatief directe

title: Learning by Doing: IFLA Futures Club #5
raw_text: The fifth edition of the IFLA Futures Club offered an opportunity to explore what it looks like to apply futures thinking in libraries, in reality. Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the Dutch National Library (KB) joined us to talk about their experience of running a concerted initiative to make futures thinking a more central part of the institution’s work, both with a view to shaping a new policy plan, and building skills more broadly. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. But with awareness that we are in a time where pre-existing ideas and assumptions are being challenged – epistemic turbulence – the Library’s new leadership was ready to take this work up a gear. There was an awareness from the start that this work provided an opportunity to think more broadly. First of all, an initaitive like this in the KB is not just an internal exercise, but also has potential impacts across the wider library field. National libraries usually have a kind of leadership within their fields, but the Dutch one has a formal role in supporting the country’s network of national libraries. What it does has the possibility to feed into changes across every local authority in the country. But beyond this, libraries are uniquely well suited for a more exploratory approach, rather than one purely focuse

title: Vijf vragen aan Saskia Vlaar: ‘AI leer je niet uit een boek, maar in de praktijk’
raw_text: Na ruim drie jaar neemt Saskia Vlaar afscheid als bestuurslid van AIC4NL. In die periode zag ze de Nederlandse AI Coalitie en AiNed samengaan, groeide AIC4NL verder als organisatie en kwamen programma’s voor innovatie, talent en toepassing steeds meer tot uitvoering. Vanuit haar achtergrond in het bedrijfsleven stelde Saskia daarbij steeds de vraag: hoe zorgen we dat AI niet bij plannen en beleid blijft, maar daadwerkelijk terechtkomt bij de mensen en organisaties die ermee aan de slag gaan? 1. Waar en wanneer begon voor jou de reis met AIC4NL, en wat sprak je aan in de opgave? “In maart 2023 werd ik gevraagd voor het bestuur. Vanuit mijn werk bij Shell op het gebied van digitale innovatie zag ik hoe afhankelijk Nederland en Europa waren van technologie uit China en de Verenigde Staten. Dat werd ooit heel tastbaar toen een gezichtsherkenningstool in het lab mij classificeerde als een vrouw van Chinese afkomst van achter in de zestig. De database waarop het systeem was getraind, bleek afkomstig uit Azië. Voor mij raakte dat aan een veel grotere vraag: zorgen we dat Nederland en Europa zelf positie opbouwen in AI, op een manier die past bij onze normen, waarden en regelgeving? Daar wilde ik aan bijdragen. Ook de expertise van Willem Jonker en Inald Lagendijk op het gebied van AI en digitalisering en de mogelijkheid om gezamenlijk aan zo’n missie te werken, spraken me aan.” 2. title: Vijf vragen aan Willem Jonker: ‘Met AI Fair Tech kan Europa zelf de koers bepalen’
raw_text: Bij zijn afscheid als bestuursvoorzitter van AIC4NL kijkt Willem Jonker terug op vier jaar waarin AI doorbrak bij het grote publiek. Het vroeg om voortdurende bijsturing van programma’s, een krachtenbundeling van organisaties en een sterkere Europese aanpak. Wat is er in beweging gebracht en wat is er nodig om Nederland verder te brengen? 1. Waar en wanneer begon voor jou de reis, en wat sprak je aan in de opgave? “Op 1 november 2022 begon ik bij AiNed. Eind november verscheen ChatGPT. Hiermee kwam AI plotseling midden in de schijnwerpers te staan, niet alleen bij vakgenoten, maar ook bij het grote publiek. Dit had direct invloed op het AiNed-programma. Bij het schrijven daarvan stond de enorme invloed van generatieve AI nog niet zo stevig op de radar. Dus werk aan de winkel. Dat is kenmerkend voor mijn afgelopen vier jaar bij AiNed en AIC4NL: de ontwikkelingen gaan zo snel dat je voortdurend moet beoordelen of je als organisatie de juiste dingen doet om AI in Nederland op een hoger plan te brengen.” 2.
